text: Your phone battery doesn't store electricity. It stores lithium ions in a high-energy spot. So how does that power your phone?
Inside is a sandwich. On one side, graphite, packed with lithium. On the other, a metal oxide. In between, a liquid that lets ions through, but not electrons.
When you use your phone, lithium ions swim across to the metal oxide. Their electrons can't follow, so they take the long way, through your phone. That flow is the current.
Charging runs it backwards. The charger pushes the ions back into the graphite, like winding a spring.
But there's wear. Heat, and holding the battery at one hundred percent, strain the graphite and slowly trap lithium so it can't come back.
Quick test. Which habit keeps a battery healthiest? A, always charging to a hundred. B, staying between twenty and eighty. Or C, draining to zero? Think!
B. Both extremes stress the cell. Staying in the middle, and keeping it cool, can make a battery last far longer.
Two tips. Never leave your phone in a hot car, or under a pillow while it charges. And turn on your phone's optimized or limit-charge setting, if it has one.
Watch again, and count the ions that cross.
